\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Refraction}, answer={B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: ray path in an atmosphere with refractive index varying with altitude | steps: Snell law in spherical shell n r sin theta constant; condition for circular ray around the planet; relation for n(h); check options | I: Bouguer invariant in a spherical atmosphere}]
On a spherical planet, the refractive index of atmosphere, as a function of altitude $h$ above the surface varies as
\[n(h)=\dfrac{n_0}{1+\dfrac{h}{2R}}\]
Where $n_0$ is a constant. A laser beam directed horizontally but an arbitrary altitude follows a trajectory that circles the planet.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Radius of planet has a magnitude $R\sqrt2$}
\opt{B}{Radius of planet has a magnitude $2R$}
\opt{C}{At a height $R\sqrt2$ from the surface of planet, refractive index is $\dfrac{n_0}{2}$}
\opt{D}{At a height $R$ from surface, refractive index is $\dfrac{2n_0}{3}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P1-PHY-S2-Q10, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=1, qno=10, type=multi, subtopic={Refraction}, answer={B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K1 S3 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: path of a light ray in a medium whose index changes with y | steps: n(y) sin theta = constant; ray equation; critical point where ray turns; time or distance; check | I: refractive index gradient gives continuous bending}]
The refractive index of the medium within a certain region $x>0$, $y>0$, changes continuously with $y$. A thin light ray travelling in air in the $x$-direction strikes the medium at right angles and moves through the medium along a circular arc of radius $R$.
\bfig{175.6}{SI01_p1_phy_s2_q10_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Refractive index of medium varies with $y$ as \bfigi{92.7}{SI01_p1_phy_s2_q10_2.png}}
\opt{B}{Refractive index of medium varies with $y$ as \bfigi{92.7}{SI01_p1_phy_s2_q10_3.png}}
\opt{C}{If refractive index of medium can increase upto a value $n=2.5$, the maximum value of $y$ is $\dfrac{3R}{5}$}
\opt{D}{If refractive index of medium can increase upto a value $n=2.5$, the maximum value of $y$ is $5R$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P2-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=single, subtopic={Lenses}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: focal length, an equiconvex lens at an opening with liquid or gas | steps: lens maker formula with different media on two sides; combined focal length; evaluate}]
An equiconvex lens of focal-length 10 cm (in air) and refractive index 3/2 is put at a small opening on a tube of length 1m fully filled with liquid of refractive index 4/3. A concave mirror of radius of curvature 20 cm is cut into two halves $m_1$ and $m_2$ and placed at the end of the tube. $m_1$ and $m_2$ are placed such that their principal axes AB and CD respectively are separated by 1mm each from the principle axes of the lens. A slit S placed in air illuminates the lens with light of frequency $7.5\times10^{14}$ Hz(in air). The light reflected from $m_1$ and $m_2$ forms interference pattern on the left end EF of the tube taking lens surface as screen. O is an opaque substance to cover the hole left by $m_1$ and $m_2$. The width of the fringes on EF.
\bfig{139.2}{SI01_p2_phy_s1_q02_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{180$\mu$m}
\opt{B}{220$\mu$m}
\opt{C}{120$\mu$m}
\opt{D}{60$\mu$m}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI05-P1-PHY-S1-Q06, source={Score-I - Test 05 (22 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=6, type=multi, subtopic={Reflection}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: images, two inclined plane mirrors as angle varies | steps: number of images 360/theta - 1; positions of images by repeated reflection; rotate mirror; check | I: images from multiple reflections}]
Two plane mirrors M$_1$ and M$_2$ are inclined at an angle `$\theta$' which can be varied by rotating the mirrors as shown in figure.
\bfig{133.0}{SI05_p1_phy_s1_q06_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}

\opt{B}{If a ray of light strikes the mirror M$_1$ at $30^\circ$ from the normal to M$_1$ then angle of deviation suffered by ray is always $360^\circ$ (consider the rays strikes only once on both mirrors)}
\opt{C}{If angle between the mirror is $30^\circ$ and the ray strikes mirror M$_1$ at $70^\circ$ to the mirror then net deviation suffered by the ray is $300^\circ$. (consider the rays strikes only once on both mirror).}

\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI05-P1-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 05 (22 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=single, subtopic={Reflection}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: speed, image of an object moving toward a convex mirror | steps: mirror formula image position; differentiate v with respect to u; velocity of image; evaluate | I: image speed from differentiated mirror formula}]
An object lies on the principal axis of a convex mirror of focal length $f=1.0$ m at a distance $3f$ from it. At time $t=0$, the object starts moving with velocity components $v_0=1$ m/s along the principal axis (towards the mirror) and $v_0=1$ m/s perpendicular to the principal axis. The image moves along the line $ax+by=c$ (where a, b and c are relatively prime integers and $x$ and $y$ are in meters.) Match the quantities given in List--I with their magnitudes (in SI units) in List--II. We are only concerned with the time in which the rays from the object to the mirror are paraxial.
\bfig{174.4}{SI05_p1_phy_s2_q08_1.png}
\begin{center}\small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{|c|p{4.8cm}|c|c|}
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{|c|}{List-I} & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{List-II}\\ \hline
(P) & Axial component of velocity of image at time $t=0$ & (1) & 1/3\\ \hline
(Q) & Transverse component of velocity of image at time $t=0$ & (2) & 1/16\\ \hline
(R) & The value of $1/a$ & (3) & 1/4\\ \hline
(S) & The value of $1/c$ & (4) & 1/6\\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{P $\to$ 2;Q $\to$ 3;R $\to$ 3;S $\to$ 1}
\opt{B}{P $\to$ 1;Q $\to$ 3;R $\to$ 4;S $\to$ 2}
\opt{C}{P $\to$ 2;Q $\to$ 4;R $\to$ 4;S $\to$ 1}
\opt{D}{P $\to$ 1;Q $\to$ 3;R $\to$ 2;S $\to$ 4}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI05-P1-PHY-S2-Q10, source={Score-I - Test 05 (22 Jan 2022)}, paper=1, qno=10, type=single, subtopic={Refraction}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: ray path in a slab, refractive index varying with y | steps: n(y) sin theta constant; ray equation; turning point; exit position; evaluate | I: Snell invariant in a graded index slab}]
A slab occupies the region between $y=0$ and $y=R=1$ m. Rays of light traveling in the XY plane enter the slab at the origin at angle of incidence $i$ and are found to travel in circular paths. Consider the following cases:

Case 1 : The refractive index of the slab, $\mu$, varies from 1 at $y=0$ to infinity at $y=R$ and $i=90$.

Case 2 : The refractive index of the slab, $\mu$, varies from infinity at $y=0$ to 1 at $y=R$ and $i=0$.
\bfig{139.4}{SI05_p1_phy_s2_q10_1.png}
\begin{center}\small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{|c|p{3.4cm}|c|c|}
\hline
\multicolumn{2}{|c|}{List-I} & \multicolumn{2}{c|}{List-II}\\ \hline
(P) & In case 1, $1/\mu$ at $y=R/4$ & (1) & 4/5\\ \hline
(Q) & In case 1, $x$ at $y=2R/5$ & (2) & 1/5\\ \hline
(R) & In case 2, $1/\mu$ at $y=R/2$ & (3) & 3/4\\ \hline
(S) & In case 2, $x$ at $y=3R/5$ & (4) & 1/2\\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{P $\to$ 4;Q $\to$ 1;R $\to$ 2;S $\to$ 3}
\opt{B}{P $\to$ 1;Q $\to$ 4;R $\to$ 3;S $\to$ 2}
\opt{C}{P $\to$ 2;Q $\to$ 2;R $\to$ 1;S $\to$ 4}
\opt{D}{P $\to$ 3;Q $\to$ 1;R $\to$ 4;S $\to$ 2}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI10-P1-PHY-S1-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 10 (24 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Refraction}, answer={A,B,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S3 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: Snell invariant in a graded medium, geometry of a circular arc | steps: mu sin(angle with y axis) is constant so mu=1/sin; circle of radius R gives sin=(R-y)/R and hence mu=R/(R-y); direction at y=R/2 from the tangent to the circle; mu=2.5 gives cos(theta max)=2/5; check sine option | I1: applying the invariant to a ray curving in a graded medium}]

The material with the greatest known refractive index is diamond, but even the refractive index of this material does not reach the value $\mu_{\max}=2.5$. It is this limit that sets the maximum angular size of the arc the light ray can cover. Angular size of arc is the angle subtended by the arc at the centre. \opt{C}{The maximum angular size of the arc of light is $\theta_{\max}$. The value of $\cos\theta_{\max}=2/5$}
\opt{D}{The maximum angular size of the arc of light is $\theta_{\max}$. The value of $\sin\theta_{\max}=2/5$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SA10-P1-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score Advanced - Test 10 (06 May 2023)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={Prisms}, answer={C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=2, diff_parts={K1 S1 I0 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: parts of a prism spectroscope | steps: collimator; prism table}]
The common prism spectroscope is shown in figure is generally made up of three parts, viz., a prism and two telescopes. One of these telescopes is used to render the rays which fall on the prism parallel to each other, and is therefore called the collimator, the other telescope is made movable so that it can be turned into the proper direction for observing any desired color, and is, therefore, called the view-telescope. A circular scale is also provided to measure angular position of telescope. On the circular scale 29 divisions of the main scale exactly coincide with the 30 divisions of the vernier scale. The smallest division of the main scale is half-a-degree (0.5\textdegree). Initially view-telescope is focused to collect rays directly from collimator and position of telescope is measured. This is position (1). Now a prism is placed as shown in the figure and telescope is focused for red, yellow and violet. The respective positions of telescope are (2), (3) and (4).\par
{\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{2pt}\noindent\begin{tabular}{|l|c|c|}
\hline
 & Reading of main scale & Reading of veriner scale\\ \hline
Position (1) & 20.0\textdegree & 20\\ \hline
Position (2) & 30.0\textdegree & 16\\ \hline
Position (3) & 32.5\textdegree & 9\\ \hline
Position (4) & 33.5\textdegree & 11\\ \hline
\end{tabular}}\par

\begin{bankq}[id=SA30-P1-PHY-S2-Q09, source={Score Advanced - Test 30 (04 May 2024)}, paper=1, qno=9, type=multi, subtopic={Refraction}, answer={A,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: melting ice hemisphere with a given heat transfer rate: light rays  apparent size | steps: ice hemisphere as a lens; rate of melting from heat transfer; radius decreases with time; refraction through the hemisphere; image position change with R; compute | C: time dependent radius and refraction through a hemisphere}]
An ice hemisphere with radius R and refractive index n lies on a warm flat table and melts slowly. The rate of heat transfer from the table to the ice is proportional to the area of contact between them. It is known that the ice hemisphere completely melts in time T$_0$. Throughout the process, a laser beam is incident on the ice from above. The beam is vertically incident at a distance of R/2 from the axis of symmetry (see figure).\par
Assume that the temperature of the ice and the surrounding atmosphere are 0$^\circ$C and remains constant during the melting process. The laser beam does not transfer energy to the ice. The melting water immediately flows off the table, and the ice does not move along the table.\par
\bfig{101.5}{SA30_p1_phy_s2_q09_1.png}
\bfig{103.2}{SA30_p1_phy_s2_q09_2.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The value of x$_0$ (point on the table where the laser beam strikes at t = 0) is $\dfrac{2\mathrm R}{\left(\sqrt{12n^2-3}+1\right)}$.}
\opt{B}{The value of x$_0$ (point on the table where the laser beam strikes at t = 0) is $\dfrac{2\mathrm R}{\left(\sqrt{4n^2-3}+1\right)}$.}
\opt{C}{The height of ice z at any time t is z = R$\left(1-\dfrac{\mathrm t^2}{\mathrm T_0^2}\right)$.}
\opt{D}{The time at which the value of x (point on the table where the laser beam strikes) becomes $\dfrac{\mathrm R}2$ is $\dfrac{\sqrt3}2$T$_0$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\[v=\mu_1\left[\frac1{\mu_1}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac1{\mu_2}\frac{dy}{dt}\right]\]

Origin as well as $x$ \& $y$ axis are considered as per sign convention.

\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS07-P2-PHY-S3-Q01, source={TNAS - Test 07 (20 Aug 2023)}, paper=2, qno=1, type=numerical, subtopic={Refraction}, answer={1.50}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: magnification of a hemispherical lens | steps: refraction at the curved surface; apparent size; ratio}]
If you place the flat side of a hemispherical glass object (lens) against a paper, it is possible to see a magnified image of the paper's surface around the center of the lens. How many times is the image bigger than the object if you are observing at a distance that is much bigger than the dimensions of the lens? The refractive index of glass is $n=1.5$.
\end{bankq}
